A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MILCO study and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained content can be matched across pagination and table renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval results, training and architecture ablations, pruning experiments, and additional appendix evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds dense control models, retrieval-efficiency measurements, and appendix analyses of view weighting and alignment-language coverage.

M1.justification: The multilingual connector, dual-view LexEcho head, sparse alignment objective and contrastive training remain unchanged. Dense variants are comparison baselines, and the weighting sweep and Seismic retrieval setup are evaluation additions rather than revisions to the proposed MILCO architecture.

E1.justification: The training corpora, benchmark suite and language coverage are retained. New efficiency measurements reuse English MIRACL, and the appendix analyses reuse existing languages and MIRACL settings; MIRACL-HN was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds two matched-backbone dense comparators: MILCO-dense with alignment plus distillation, and with distillation only. The broader baseline roster remains. BGE-M3 All disappears from the MKQA summary Table 4 but remains in the corresponding detailed comparison, v2 Table 9.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation beyond effectiveness and sparsity with single-core CPU benchmarking of Seismic and Faiss HNSW, reporting mean/P95 latency, throughput and index size. It also introduces matched-backbone/data dense controls and a pivot/source weighting sweep. Existing benchmark protocols and MILCO training hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.10 tests sensitivity to pivot/source weighting, while A.11 groups existing languages by alignment-data share and analyzes gains over a dense control. Section 6 also extends pruning analysis to measured speed and storage tradeoffs. These substantially expand the diagnostic evidence beyond v1's component ablations, examples and sparsity curves.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 and retain the same uncertainty-reporting practices. No new repeated-run information, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. The new P95 latency is a performance metric, not an estimate of uncertainty in the results.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores remain, including MILCO's 72.3 MIRACL nDCG@10. Substantial new results include dense-control scores of 67.9 and 70.9, latency/storage measurements in Table 5, weighting results of 5.61 for source-only versus 72.66 for balanced fusion in Table 19, and coverage-group gains of 1.59 versus 0.77 in Table 20. These are added results, not same-setting improvements to retained scores.

T1.justification: The architectural definitions, sparse-aware MSE objective and distillation formulation in Section 3 and Appendix A.7 are unchanged. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added; the new weighting and grouping descriptions specify empirical analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add explicit claims of 3× lower retrieval latency and 10× smaller index size alongside the retained 30-active-dimension effectiveness claim. The central architectural contributions, multilingual retrieval claims and conclusion otherwise retain their scope.

C2.justification: New interpretations concern operational efficiency, the essential role of the pivot view, tolerance to approximately balanced fusion, and transfer to languages absent from alignment data. Appendix A.11 also identifies a negative Farsi gap. Existing explanations of semantic collapse, rare-entity preservation and comparison-fairness limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies CPU hardware and index parameters for the new efficiency experiment, identifies the dense alignment teacher, and reports per-language alignment counts. Anonymous code access becomes a named GitHub project, and promised checkpoints become a stated release. Existing training-detail tables are retained; external availability was not checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds Douze et al. (2024), The Faiss Library, to support the efficiency experiment. The related-work discussion and positioning of MILCO's novelty remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes include localized terminology and copyediting, a conference-publication header, acknowledgments, expanded efficiency discussion, and new Appendices A.10–A.11. The original section order and most existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds latency Table 5 and appendix Tables 19–21, expands Table 1, and shortens the MKQA summary table. Figures 4–5 move, the language-list table becomes more compact, and subsequent tables are renumbered. Existing figures and the overall presentation template remain substantially intact.

improvement.justification: Matched dense controls, direct latency/storage measurements and additional ablations strengthen validation, while the stated checkpoint release improves reproducibility. However, the abstract combines the 30-token effectiveness result with 3×/10× efficiency figures from a separate English-only, pivot-view experiment at p=60. Table 5 reports 50.3 nDCG@10 there versus Qwen3's 50.4. The added evidence improves the paper, but does not establish the combined headline claim under one setting.
